prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

You ever wake up with your footie PJs warming your neck like a noose? Ever upchuck after a home-cooked meal? Or notice how the blood on the bottoms of your feet just won’t seem to go away? Love, it used to be you could retire your toothbrush for like two or three days and still I’d push my downy face into your neck. Used to be I hung on your every word. (Sing! you’d say: and I was a bird.Freedom! you’d say: and I never really knew what that meant, but liked the way it rang like a rusty bell.) Used to be. But now I can tell you your breath stinks and you’re full of shit. You have more lies about yourself than bodies beneath your bed. Rootingfor the underdog. Team player. Hook, line and sinker. Love, you helped design the brick that built the walls around the castle in the basement of which is a vault inside of which is another vault inside of which . . . you get my point. Your tongue is made of honey but flicks like a snake’s. Voice like a bird but everyone’s ears are bleeding. From the inside your house shines and shines, but from outside you can see it’s built from bones. From out here it looks like a graveyard, and the garden’s all ash. And besides, your breath stinks. We’re through.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker recalls once loving and admiring their partner despite their flaws.
- The speaker has become disillusioned and now recognizes the partner’s dishonesty and hypocrisy.
- The partner’s charming words and outward beauty conceal cruelty, violence, and corruption.
- Images of bodies, bones, blood, vaults, and ash portray the relationship as oppressive and death-ridden.
- The speaker ultimately rejects the partner and ends the relationship.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

A disillusioned lover confronts a deceitful, destructive partner through darkly comic, grotesque imagery contrasting past devotion with present disgust. The speaker recognizes that the partner’s charm conceals lies, violence, and moral decay, and ends the relationship as an act of clarity and liberation.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: You, PJs, Ever

outputs.L1:
Do you ever wake up with your footie pajamas warming your neck like a noose? Ever upchuck after a home-cooked meal? Or notice how the blood on the bottoms of your feet just won’t seem to go away?

Love, it used to be that you could retire your toothbrush for two or three days, and still I’d press my downy face into your neck. It used to be that I hung on your every word. (“Sing!” you’d say, and I was a bird. “Freedom!” you’d say, and I never really knew what that meant, but I liked the way it rang, like a rusty bell.)

Used to be.

But now I can tell you that your breath stinks and you’re full of shit. You have more lies about yourself than bodies beneath your bed: rooting for the underdog, team player, hook, line, and sinker.

Love, you helped design the brick that built the walls around the castle, in the basement of which is a vault, inside of which is another vault, inside of which . . . you get my point.

Your tongue is made of honey, but it flicks like a snake’s. Your voice is like a bird’s, but everyone’s ears are bleeding. From the inside, your house shines and shines; from the outside, you can see that it’s built from bones. From out here, it looks like a graveyard, and the garden is all ash.

And besides, your breath stinks.

We’re through.
outputs.L2:
Have you ever come to with the collar of your one-piece pajamas cinched around your throat? Have you ever vomited after eating something prepared in your own kitchen? Have you wondered why the stains under your feet—blood, unmistakably—refuse to wash off?

Darling, there was a time when you could skip brushing your teeth for several days and I would still nestle my soft cheek against your neck. Back then, I believed everything you said. You told me to make music, and I became something winged. You spoke of liberty; I didn’t understand it, but the word pleased me, clanging with the charm of an old corroded bell.

That was before.

Now I’m able to say plainly that your mouth reeks and everything you say is garbage. The false stories you tell about who you are outnumber the corpses hidden beneath your bed: champion of the overlooked, cooperative companion, total believer. Sweetheart, you had a hand in shaping the very masonry used to raise the barriers around a fortress whose cellar contains a safe, which holds another safe, which conceals yet another—and so on. You understand.

Your words taste sugary, though your tongue strikes with a serpent’s speed. You sound as lovely as a songbird, yet your listeners hemorrhage within their ears. Seen from the interior, your home glitters endlessly; viewed from the street, its skeleton is literal. At this distance, the place resembles a burial ground, with nothing but cinders where the flowers should grow.

Also, your breath is foul.

This is over.
outputs.L3:
The speaker recalls a time when they genuinely loved and admired their partner, accepting their flaws and overlooking their darker qualities. Once captivated by the partner’s charm and beauty, the speaker viewed them with affection and trust. Over time, however, this admiration gives way to profound disillusionment. The speaker begins to recognize the partner’s dishonesty and hypocrisy, realizing that their appealing exterior masks a deeply corrupt nature.

The contrast between appearance and reality is central to the speaker’s change of heart. The partner’s charming words and outward beauty may seem attractive, but they conceal cruelty, violence, and moral decay. Disturbing images of bodies, bones, blood, vaults, and ash reinforce this realization. These images create an atmosphere of confinement and death, suggesting that the relationship has become oppressive, destructive, and emotionally suffocating.

Ultimately, the speaker refuses to remain deceived or controlled. Having seen through the partner’s false appearance and recognized the harm beneath it, they decisively reject the partner and bring the relationship to an end.
outputs.L4:
I used to mistake your charm for kindness. You had a way of entering a room as though you had brought the light with you, and I was foolish enough to stand in it, grateful for the warmth. I defended every contradiction, excused every wound, and polished your promises until they shone like truth. Even when the people who loved me warned that something was wrong, I insisted they simply did not know you as I did.

They were right. I did not know you at all.

Your sweetness was only paint over rot. Beneath the polished smile was a mouth crowded with lies, each one waiting for its turn to bite. You treated tenderness like a weakness to exploit and trust like a small animal you could torment when bored. Wherever you went, you left damage behind—broken friendships, frightened silences, apologies extracted from people who had done nothing wrong. Then you stood among the wreckage looking wounded, as if destruction were an unfortunate weather pattern that happened to follow you.

Once, I found your confidence irresistible. Now it reminds me of a rat wearing a crown in a flooded cellar: ridiculous, filthy, and convinced the kingdom is his. Your compliments stink of calculation. Your tears arrive on cue. Even your affection feels like something damp and spoiled pulled from the back of a cupboard and served on a silver plate.

For too long, I called my endurance devotion. I believed that loving you meant forgiving everything: the betrayals, the threats, the cruelty disguised as humor, the sudden flashes of violence followed by gifts and soft words. I kept waiting for the person I first met to return. But that person was only a costume, and you wore it until you were certain I would stay.

I will not stay.

I see you clearly now—not as the tragic hero of your own inventions, not as the wounded soul I imagined I could save, but as someone who chooses harm and then lies about the blood on their hands. Whatever beauty I once found in you has curdled. Whatever power you held over me depended on my confusion, and that confusion is gone.

So keep your promises. Feed them to the next person who mistakes glitter for gold. Keep your apologies, your rehearsed sorrow, and your poisonous little miracles. I am leaving with nothing of yours except the lesson.

You will say I abandoned you. You will say I was cruel. You may invent a hundred stories in which you are innocent and I am ungrateful. Tell them all. I no longer need to defend myself inside your theater.

The door is open. The air beyond it is cold, clean, and entirely my own. I step through without looking back.
outputs.L5:
**You. PJs. Ever.**

Meet the comfiest PJs you’ll ever own—made for slow mornings, cozy nights, and every relaxing moment in between. Soft, effortless, and designed with You in mind, they’re more than pajamas. They’re your new favorite way to unwind.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, darkly comic breakup monologue in which the speaker addresses a deceptive lover, using grotesque domestic imagery, repeated references to bad breath, and escalating metaphors about hidden bodies, vaults, bones, and ash.
counterfactuals.output:
You said there was no one else, but your toothbrush kept coming home with lipstick on its knees.

Don’t interrupt. Your breath is bad.

It has always been bad. Not ordinary bad, not garlic or graveyard or the warm sigh of a dog dreaming under a radiator. Your breath smells like a refrigerator unplugged during a divorce. It smells like milk learning a secret. Every time you whispered *I love you*, the wallpaper curled away from us and the fruit bowl filled with flies out of professional courtesy.

Still, I stayed.

I scrubbed your promises from the bathtub with a wire brush. I boiled your alibis in the good saucepan. I found someone else’s earring in the butter dish and let you tell me it was a silver comma that had fallen out of a sentence. How grammatical of you. How delicate. How absolutely typical that even your punctuation was sleeping around.

And your breath—God. Your bad breath stood between us like a damp priest. It blessed every lie. It fogged the windows from the inside. Some mornings I woke convinced a small country had collapsed in your mouth overnight, leaving its livestock, parliament, and sewage system to rot behind your teeth.

You said I was imagining things.

So I imagined the body under the kitchen floor.

At first it was only metaphorical: a little corpse of trust tucked beneath the linoleum, knees politely drawn to its chest. But then you started pacing whenever the floorboards creaked. You bought rugs. So many rugs. Rugs over rugs, a whole woolen bureaucracy dedicated to covering one suspicious rectangle.

I asked, “Who is she?”

You said, “Who is who?”

Your breath answered first. It came out carrying a shovel.

Then I imagined more bodies. One in the pantry behind the flour. One folded into the sofa where the loose change goes. One standing upright in the broom closet, wearing my robe and your expression. Soon the whole apartment was crowded with the dead versions of me: the me who believed you on Tuesday, the me who forgave you on Friday, the me who apologized for finding evidence.

They were very quiet roommates. Cleaner than you.

But you, darling, were not merely hiding bodies. No. That would be almost quaint. You were building a vault.

I could hear it growing behind your ribs: steel doors, spinning locks, little numbered drawers. In one drawer, her name. In another, the hotel receipt. In another, the exact tone you used when you told me I was crazy. You swallowed the combination and smiled.

Bad idea, smiling. Your breath escaped.

It smelled like the vault had flooded. Like all your secrets were floating facedown in black water, bumping gently against the ceiling.

And beneath the vault—bones.

Not one skeleton. An architecture of bones. Femurs for pillars, finger bones for chandeliers, teeth mortared into the walls. Every lie you told had calcified there. Every “late meeting,” every “dead battery,” every “you’re the only one” became another white strut holding up the mansion of your innocence.

You lived in it comfortably. You hung curtains. You invited me over.

“Make yourself at home,” you said, with that catastrophic breath, while somewhere under the dining table a rib cage played the xylophone.

Well, I’m leaving.

Not because of her, exactly. Not because of the earrings, the receipts, the rugs, the imaginary bodies becoming less imaginary by the hour. I’m leaving because I finally understand: you don’t have a heart. You have a crematorium with excellent manners.

Everything I gave you went in warm and came out ash.

My patience: ash.

My appetite: ash.

That summer in Lisbon: a teaspoon of ash in a souvenir jar.

Even now you’re opening your mouth to explain, and I can smell the furnace. Your bad breath rolls toward me, hot and gray, carrying the ashes of every person foolish enough to stand close while you said *trust me*.

So keep the apartment. Keep the rugs. Keep your bone palace and your flooded vault and the little republic decomposing behind your teeth.

I’ve packed my things.

The blue suitcase contains my clothes. The red one contains my dignity. The black one is making a noise, but that is no longer my problem.

If anyone asks, tell them we wanted different things.

I wanted honesty.

You wanted somewhere to hide the shovel.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a prose poem that begins with three unsettling rhetorical questions, nostalgically recalls a relationship’s better days, then turns into a blunt denunciation ending with “We’re through.”
counterfactuals.output:
Who has been breathing behind the walls at night? Why do the mirrors keep remembering your face after you leave? If love is dead, what keeps dragging its chair across the floor?

Once, we were summer windows thrown open to rain, laughing as the curtains billowed and the whole bright world seemed willing to enter. You tasted of coffee and promises; I knew the map of your hands, the warm country of your shoulder. We missed trains on purpose. We danced barefoot in the kitchen. Even silence was tender then, a small animal sleeping between us.

But you turned tenderness into leverage. You lied, withheld, blamed, and returned only when loneliness bruised your pride. You made an altar of my patience and demanded sacrifice after sacrifice. Enough. I will not call cruelty confusion or cowardice sorrow. Take your ghosts, your excuses, your practiced apologies. We’re through.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental breakup letter in a conversational voice. Mix tenderness with horror imagery, include parenthetical memories about singing and freedom, use fragmented phrases like “Team player” and “Hook, line and sinker,” and portray the lover’s beautiful home as secretly built from bones.
counterfactuals.output:
Hey you,

I’m leaving.

There. Plain as a plate on the table. Plain as the little white moon of toothpaste you always left in the sink.

I don’t mean I’m leaving for milk, or air, or one of my midnight walks where I stand beneath the power lines and pretend their humming is the universe trying to remember my name. I mean I’m taking my books, the blue cup, the sweater you hate. I mean I won’t be coming back to this beautiful house.

And it is beautiful. God, you made it beautiful.

The yellow curtains. The warm floors. The staircase polished to a dark shine, winding upward like a promise.

But I know now what’s underneath.

Bones.

Not metaphorical bones, darling. Not “the bones of the house are good.” I mean ribs fitted beneath the plaster. Knuckles mortared into the chimney. A spine where the main beam should be. At night, when the heat comes on, teeth chatter inside the walls.

You said it was the pipes.

I wanted to believe you.

Hook, line and sinker.

That was us, wasn’t it? Me swallowing the glittering thing because it came from your hand. You calling it love while the line tightened.

(Do you remember singing in the car, windows down, both of us getting every word wrong? I thought freedom sounded like that—your voice breaking, my hair whipping into my mouth, the highway opening its black ribbon ahead of us.)

I’m not saying you’re a monster.

That would be easier.

Monsters don’t make coffee exactly right. Monsters don’t kiss the scar on your knee. Monsters don’t say, Come here, honey, and mean it—at least for a minute.

You were tender with me. You were terrible with me. Sometimes in the same breath.

Team player.

That’s what you called me when I stopped asking why the basement door was locked. When I smiled at dinner while something scratched beneath the floorboards. When I helped you hang pictures over the places where the walls bulged outward, as if the house were full and trying not to be sick.

I kept the peace.

I kept your secrets.

I kept hearing footsteps after you fell asleep.

(Once, in the kitchen, we sang so loudly the glasses trembled in the cabinet. You spun me barefoot across the tiles. I remember thinking: no cage could hold a sound like this. I remember not noticing the tiles were tiny, ivory-colored, each one shaped like a tooth.)

I loved you. I need you to know that.

Maybe I still do, in the stupid animal way a severed hand still tries to close.

But love shouldn’t require this much bleaching.

So I’m leaving the key on the counter. I’m leaving the roses in their vase, though the water has gone pink. I’m leaving the bed with its carved headboard, its soft sheets, its quiet little pulse.

Keep the house.

Keep its elegant jaw.

Keep every room that learned how to pronounce my fear.

I’m going somewhere badly built and honest. Somewhere with crooked shelves, thin walls, ordinary foundations. Somewhere the night noises are only mice, only rain, only branches brushing the glass.

And if I sing there, I’ll sing alone at first.

Then louder.

Then free.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Gothic, absurdist monologue spoken to a manipulative partner whose charming words conceal lies and violence. Make the language lyrical but visceral, with images of bloody feet, a rusty bell, nested vaults, a snake-like tongue, bleeding ears, and an ash-filled garden.
counterfactuals.output:
You call me *darling* as if the word were a white glove, and not the little shroud you pull over every bruise.

How charmingly you speak. Even now, your voice arrives perfumed, bowing at the door, carrying roses stolen from graves. But I have learned what kneels inside your syllables. I have seen your tongue slip loose behind your teeth—long, patient, snake-like—testing the air for weakness, tasting where the truth has cracked.

Do not smile. Your smile is only a window painted on a wall.

I walked to you on bloody feet. I crossed corridors that lengthened out of spite, staircases that led downward no matter which way I climbed. Above me, a rusty bell kept ringing without a hand, without a rope, without a church. Each toll said: *Believe him.* Each toll said: *You made him do it.* Each toll shook red dust from the rafters until my ears began to bleed.

Still, you whispered that the sound was music.

You have always been an architect of nested vaults. Inside each promise, a locked room. Inside that room, a coffin. Inside the coffin, another promise, smaller and sweeter, kicking faintly in the dark. I opened them all. I broke my nails on your tenderness. At the center I found nothing but a mirror wearing your face.

And behind it—your hands.

Ah, those hands. How innocent they become in daylight. How they flutter like doves when witnesses enter. Yet at midnight they remember their true religion.

You tell me the garden will bloom again. But I have stood in that garden. The fountains cough soot. The lilies are gray as old teeth. Ash fills the flowerbeds, ash fills the birdbath, ash drifts through the hedges in the shape of children who have forgotten their names. You planted apologies there and watered them with my fear. Nothing grew except silence.

No more.

Keep your velvet words. Feed them to the bell. Let it choke on them until its iron throat splits. Keep your roses, your mirrors, your little coffins of devotion. I am done mistaking the lock for shelter.

Tonight I leave your house of endless interiors. I leave barefoot if I must, though the stones open me again. Let the path drink what blood remains. Every footprint will be a red mouth saying what you never could:

*This happened.*

*You knew.*

*I survived you.*

And when you call after me—darling, darling, darling—I will not turn. I will hear only the serpent dragging itself through dead leaves, searching for a warmer lie.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a sharply accusatory prose-poetry breakup speech that repeatedly calls the addressee “Love,” contrasts “Used to be” with the present, and exposes their hypocrisy through surreal metaphors before dismissing them over their stinking breath.
counterfactuals.output:
Love, you used to be a window flung open at midnight,  
a clean wind lifting the curtains of my ribs.  
Now you are the landlord boarding up the sky  
and charging me rent for the dark.

Used to be, Love, your promises wore white gloves.  
Now I see the blood under their fingernails.  
You preached honesty with a forked tongue,  
then called the echo a liar.

Love, you used to be water.  
Now you are a mirror drowning anyone  
who looks too long.  
You handed me a compass made of moth wings,  
laughed when north burned away,  
then blamed my feet for getting lost.

Used to be, I mistook your hunger for devotion.  
Now I know: you were a cathedral with a cash register,  
a saint selling counterfeit halos  
from the trunk of a rusted moon.

Love, don’t stand there polishing your innocence.  
I watched you plant knives  
and complain when the garden came up silver.  
I watched you invite winter into my bed  
and accuse me of shivering.

Used to be, Love, I answered when you called.  
Now your voice is just a cockroach  
dragging a crown across the kitchen floor.

So take your paper thunder,  
your bargain-bin miracles,  
your apologies stitched from other people’s wounds.  
Take that rotten little gospel you keep breathing in my face.

Go, Love.  
The door is open.

And close your mouth on the way out—  
your hypocrisy was ugly enough,  
but your breath stinks.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
